# Dubbhiyamakkaṭajātaka (Ja 174)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Tricky Monkey

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dubbhiyamakkaṭajātaka* (Ja 174), translated in modern scholarship as *The Tricky Monkey*, is a narrative belonging to the canonical Pali Jātaka collection [Catalog; SuttaCentral]. According to its commentary's framing narrative, the Buddha related this story while dwelling at Veḷuvana in reference to Devadatta; upon overhearing the monastic assembly in the Hall of Truth discuss Devadatta's ingratitude and treachery toward friends, the Buddha explained that Devadatta had manifested identical behavior in previous lifetimes [SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a brahmin who draws water from a well for a thirsty monkey. Rather than expressing gratitude, the sated monkey makes faces at the Bodhisatta and, when chastised, insolently boasts of the shameless nature of monkeys and threatens to defecate upon him [Appleton 2010]. Naomi Appleton cites this tale as an illustration of how non-Buddhist or immoral characters in the Jātakas sometimes get the better of the Bodhisatta through their bad behavior, making the Bodhisatta appear foolish [Appleton 2010].

The text was edited by V. Fausböll in the second volume of his Roman-script edition of the *Jātaka Together with Its Commentary*, where manuscript variants preserve alternate designations such as *Dutiyamakkaṭajātaka* [Fausböll 1879]. SuttaCentral indexes translations in four modern languages [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis via DharmaNexus registers five matching textual segments shared with the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (specifically §1.1–1.4 aligned with §413_13–416), while neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies cross-language parallels in Chinese, Tibetan, or Sanskrit corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
